19724-home-pastimes-or-tableaux-vivants:
Tableaux vivants are living pictures: costumed people holding still as famous scenes. J. H. Head's Home Pastimes teaches families how to stage them at home. The book opens on the nature of a perfect picture. It claims such pictures are appreciated wherever they are shown. Poetic feeling, it argues, shows itself the same way everywhere.

Parlor entertainment mattered before radio filled the evenings. A good tableau needed costumes, poses, curtains, and nerve. Head gives home players the craft behind the trick. Readers learn how Victorian families amused their guests. The book also preserves period taste in scenes and dress. It is a handbook from the age of the drawing-room stage.
19860-the-arabian-nights-entertainments:
The Arabian Nights Entertainments gathers the tales of the Thousand and One Nights. This 1914 edition traces the collection's deep roots. Tenth-century Arabic writers already mention a Persian book called The Thousand Nights. In it, Scheherazade wins one more day of life with each tale. Many stories show Persian or Hindu origins beneath Arabic dress. Aladdin, Sindbad, and Ali Baba live in this tradition.

No single author made the Nights; centuries of tellers did. Frame story, genies, and Baghdad streets bind hundreds of tales. English readers met them through many translations and selections. The collection shaped Western dreams of the East profoundly. It also preserves folk tales of real antiquity. Every edition is a door into that shared story-hoard.
19870-illuminated-manuscripts:
Illuminated Manuscripts introduces the art of hand-decorated books. It begins from a broad claim: the desire for decoration is as old as the human race. Nature is the source of beauty, the author argues. Something in us reproduces felt beauty in material form. That reproduction may appeal to eye or ear. Medieval gold-leaf pages are the book's great exhibit.

John W. Bradley wrote standard handbooks on medieval art crafts. Illumination joined painting, calligraphy, and goldsmith work in one page. This guide explains styles, pigments, and famous examples. It served the Victorian revival of manuscript arts. Kelmscott Press designs drew on the same love. The book remains a friendly doorway into the scriptorium.
19978-35-sonnets:
Fernando Pessoa wrote his 35 Sonnets in English, publishing them in Lisbon in 1918. One sonnet here thinks on a long-dead beloved. The speaker could not think of her as mere rotted dust. She had been long dead, yet lived entire in his seeing thought. What she was in him had never fled, he insists. The argument turns grief into metaphysics in fourteen lines.

Pessoa, Portugal's great modernist, wrote under many invented authors, called heteronyms. The sonnets are signed with his own name yet feel Shakespeare-haunted. Their English is deliberately archaic and knotted. Readers watch a Portuguese genius wrestle English tradition itself. These thirty-five poems are small, dense, and strange. They reward the slowest possible reading.
20161-sophisms-of-the-protectionists:
Sophisms of the Protectionists attacks the case for tariffs that guard home trade. A sophism is a slick argument that sounds true but is not. Free traders offered this small book at the cost of printing. They urged each reader to hand a copy to protectionist friends.

That push shows how hot the tariff fight ran in its day. Cheap imports, jobs, and prices all hung on the debate then. The book answers guard-trade claims point by point in plain words. Readers get a neat fossil of a fight that still echoes in trade politics.
20176-the-drone-a-play-in-three-acts:
Rutherford Mayne wrote The Drone, a play in three acts, published in 1912. An elderly man with a gloomy face enters a kitchen slowly. Sly humor in his eyes relieves that gloom at once. He looks at Kate, then scans the dresser with a disgusted shake.

Mayne wrote Irish plays that mix rural talk with sharp character study. A drone, in hive terms, is one who lives off others' work. That charge hangs over the men in this kitchen drama. Readers get Ulster speech, family friction, and humor with a sting in it.
20177-john-bull-or-the-englishman-s-fire:
George Colman the Younger wrote John Bull, a comedy in five acts, for the English stage. Colman defends true comedy against the pull of broad farce. Farce, he argues, has trained crowds to love hearty laughter alone. Smiles, by contrast, are now scorned as weak and insipid fare.

John Bull stands for the plain Englishman in this lively play. Colman sought a picture from real life, not mere caricature on stage. His comedy turns on money, class, and bluster in English homes. Readers get Georgian theatre with wit aimed at national pride itself.
20217-the-stranger-a-drama-in-five-acts:
The Stranger is a drama in five acts, a stage play of faith and doubt. Its preface warns how sacred faith is often badly taught in schools. Pious but ignorant teaching can breed the very doubts it fears. Infidelity may be sown where teachers meant to root it out.

Such a charge sets a grave tone for the drama that follows. A stranger's arrival in plays of this kind often tests a whole town. Belief, love, and hidden pasts tend to collide around such a figure. Readers get a serious period drama on faith taught well or ill.
20450-the-lives-of-the-fathers-martyrs-a:
The Lives of the Fathers, Martyrs, and Other Principal Saints is the great English collection of saints' lives, first made by Alban Butler. This edition adds lives written since the author's death. It aims to give readers a saint for study across the whole church year.

The editors worked to render the collection as complete as possible. They added the life of Saint Alphonsus Liguori and other saints canonized after Butler died, lives found in no earlier form of the work. Generations of Catholic readers used these volumes for daily devotion and for the stories behind feast days.
20537-the-argonauts: The Argonauts takes its title from the old seekers of the golden fleece and applies it to modern hunters of wealth. Its pages describe men working options and exchanges in many markets and corporations. Such men, the book says, need opposite qualities at once. They need the courage of the lion, the caution of the fox, and the talons of the falcon.
20543-edward-fitzgerald-and-posh-herring:
James Blyth's Edward FitzGerald and Posh tells the story of a strange friendship. FitzGerald, the poet of Omar Khayyam, grew close to Joseph Fletcher, a Lowestoft herring merchant nicknamed Posh. Blyth prints their connection and letters for the first time.

With the exception of Charles Lamb, Blyth writes, no man's letters have endeared his memory to so many readers. But the letters published before were written to cultured gentlemen, men of FitzGerald's own world. Posh was different: a working merchant of the herring fleet. The book shows the poet's warmth across the barriers of class.
20755-short-studies-on-great-subjects:
History, says the voice in Short Studies on Great Subjects, can look like a child's box of letters. We pick the letters we like, spell the word we want, and hide the rest. That sharp image opens a set of essays on grand themes.

James Anthony Froude, the famed historian, wrote studies of this kind with bold sweep. Faith, rule, sea power, and great lives pass under his gaze. He writes as a thinker, not a mere keeper of facts. Readers who like strong views in fine prose will find his essays both grand in scope and open to sharp debate.
20989-a-comedy-of-errors-in-seven-acts:
Tyrants crush distant isles and bend a worthy race under a foreign yoke, this verse drama cries. A noble charge waits within thy grasp, its speaker urges in high, old tones. A Comedy of Errors in Seven Acts speaks in that grave stage dress.

Verse, tyranny, and a helpless people's plea mark this odd, earnest play. Its seven acts promise error and tangle on a grand scale. Little is known of its stage life beyond its printed page. The book stands as a curio of amateur drama, where lofty verse and bold claims far outrun the footlights it likely never met.
21211-silverpoints:
John Gray's Silverpoints is a slim book of delicate, highly wrought poems. Elkin Mathews and John Lane published it in London in 1893 at the Bodley Head. Many carry French dedications and titles. The opening piece follows courtly ladies through an orchard, bending under low, forked branches over dew-soaked grass.

Gray was linked with the decadent writers of the 1890s, and these poems favour rare words, fine images, and slow, languid movement. A poem to Paul Verlaine appears among them. In the printed book the verse was set in italics, a design flourish this text edition notes but cannot show. Silverpoints remains Gray's best-known collection.
21253-the-swedish-norwegian-union-crisis:
K. Nordlund published this history with documents at Uppsala and Stockholm in 1905, the year Norway broke its union with Sweden. He promises a condensed account of the last few years plus extracts from the key documents. The consular question, whether Norway could have its own consuls, sits at the centre of the quarrel.

Nordlund writes from the Swedish side, answering a brochure by Fridtjof Nansen and accusing Norwegian agitation of mishandling plain facts. He traces the crisis back to the union's founding in 1814. Read today, the book shows how a constitutional dispute over trade officials nearly brought two kingdoms to war.
21396-the-three-lieutenants:
Three young officers of the Royal Navy meet again in W. H. G. Kingston's The Three Lieutenants. The book is the second in a set that begins with The Three Midshipmen. It shows life in the navy of the 1860s, when the three friends now hold higher rank.

By a happy chance, their postings let them serve near each other once more. Old Admiral Triton, now retired, still follows their careers with pride. Kingston first won fame with these books, which came out in weekly parts. Sea service, friendship, and fresh adventure fill this long tale, which ends with The Three Admirals.
21401-in-new-granada-or-heroes-and-patri:
South America's wars for freedom from Spain form the ground of W. H. G. Kingston's In New Granada. The narrator's father came from an old Covenanter family in Dumfriesshire, one of six sons. Most of those sons had to seek their luck in the wide world.

English folk are caught up in the fight of the Patriots against Spanish rule. The tale shows camp, march, and clash across a whole small country. Kingston sides with the cause of freedom, and he draws the Spanish as harsh foes. Travel, battle, and close escapes carry the story from one end of the land to the other.
21442-your-plants:
James Sheehan gives plain help for home growers in Your Plants, first entered for copyright in 1884. The full title promises care of tender and hardy plants in house and garden. The idea came to Sheehan at a large meeting of florists in western New York.

Early chapters treat lawns, potting soils, bought feeds, and the sowing of seeds. Later ones cover watering, winter storage in cellars, and the law of colour in flowers. Sheehan also explains layering, cuttings, and grafting in short, clear steps. The Orange Judd reprint of 1919 kept the book in reach of home gardeners.
21515-venice-preserved-a-tragedy-in-five:
Thomas Otway's Venice Preserved, a tragedy in five acts, is given here in an 1874 acting edition. Dio Boucicault revised the text for Booth's Theatre, with stage business, casts, and dress lists. Jaffier, Pierre, and Belvidera wear rich Venetian garb, down to plumes and rosettes.

The play turns on a plot against the senate of Venice and a friend torn two ways. Jaffier must choose between his fellow plotters and the wife he loves. The preface notes how Otway built a great work from a few thin facts of history. Few English tragedies of his age have held the stage so well.
21531-woodwork-joints:
Woodwork Joints, in the Woodworker series, teaches how joints are set out, made, and used. Four hundred pictures back the text, and an index closes the revised edition. The editor calls the range of joints unmatched in any prior book of its kind.

Teachers of handicraft get exercises of real use for class work at every level. The book treats the two secrets of good building: knowing how, and knowing why. Companion volumes in the series cover tools, staining, turning, and carving. For home workers and pros alike, the joint is where craft stands or falls, and this guide takes it joint by joint.
21570-the-squire-an-original-comedy-in-t:
Arthur W. Pinero's comedy The Squire first played at the St James's Theatre on December 29, 1881. This edition, copyrighted in 1905, prints the cast of that first night. Mrs Kendal played Kate Verity, and Mr Kendal played Lieutenant Thorndyke.

The scene is a decayed, weather-beaten Elizabethan mansion, ivy over broken stone. A secret marriage drives the first act, in a village of clergy, officers, gossips, and watchful kin. A reporter from the Pagley Mercury pokes into local affairs. Pinero, then a rising playwright, mixes romance, family secrets, and village comedy in three neat, well-made acts.
21583-children-of-the-tenements:
Jacob A. Riis tells tales of New York's poorest children in Children of the Tenements, copyrighted in 1897 and issued in 1903. Riis had written How the Other Half Lives and The Battle with the Slum. Pictures by C. M. Relyea and others show the world he describes.

Adam Grunschlag sits at his street stand in falling snow, lost in thought. Around him the holiday bustle grows, and he heeds none of it. Story by story, Riis shows barefoot kids in passageways and families crammed in dark rooms. His tales plead, without preaching, for the children the rich city forgot.
21820-oh-susannah-a-farcical-comedy-in-t:
A doctor's consulting room in Pimlico is the single scene of Oh! Susannah!, a farcical comedy in three acts by Mark Ambient. The play ran first at the Eden Theatre, Brighton, in September 1897, then at the Royalty in London. Its action is continuous, from four to six on a Lady Day afternoon. The three acts take under two hours in the playing.

The printed text gives the full stage world: whiskey decanter, medical chest, surgical knives, microscope, and a detective camera shaped like a turnip watch. Farce needs its props, and Ambient lists them all. The dialogue runs in servants' slang and drawing-room polish. It is a tidy relic of the light London stage of the 1890s.
21849-the-mind-the-paint-girl-a-comedy-i:
London's smart set talks, flirts, and schemes in The Mind the Paint Girl, a comedy in four acts by Arthur Wing Pinero, published in 1912. The cast list alone tells the story's world. A viscount, a colonel, and a German baron mix with an actress's manager and a crowd of young men about town. Pinero's name heads a long shelf of stage hits, from The Second Mrs. Tanqueray to Trelawny of the Wells.

The title comes from a warning cry in painters' studios, turned here toward a girl of the stage. Pinero builds his comedy on manners, money, and the fear of a wet-paint reputation. The printed play keeps the third-act song in full. It shows the master of the well-made play near the end of his reign.
21865-king-arthur-and-his-knights:
Arthur pulls the sword and gathers his knights in Maude L. Radford's King Arthur and His Knights, published at Chicago in 1903. Walter J. Enright's pictures show the king, the Round Table, and the Holy Grail. The tales run in order: Arthur made king, Excalibur won, Guinevere wed, and Gareth come to court unknown. Lancelot, Balin, Geraint, and Enid each take their turn at the center.

Radford retells the old legends in clear prose pitched to young readers. The search for the Holy Grail and the death of Arthur close the book, as they must. She keeps the wonder and trims the tangle. For many American children, this was the first door into Camelot, and it opens easily still.
21928-light-freights:
A night-watchman on a wharf holds court in W. W. Jacobs's Light Freights, a book of comic tales from 1901. Speaking of money, the watchman says, the world would be brighter if we all had more of it. Then he admits that being short sharpens people, and tells of the sharpest man he ever knew, who never had a ha'penny. That voice, thoughtful and sly, frames tale after tale.

The stories bear titles like Hard Labour, A Garden Plot, and The Resurrection of Mr. Wiggett. Jacobs peoples them with sailors, skippers, and schemers along the Thames. His dialogue, thick with dropped aitches, carries the comedy. Light Freights is Jacobs in his prime form: short, dry tales where human nature is the cargo and folly pays the freight.
21932-embarrassments:
Four long tales by Henry James make up Embarrassments, published in 1896, and each turns on a delicate social or artistic knot. The Figure in the Carpet opens the book: a young critic is set to review Hugh Vereker's new novel for The Middle. His friend Corvick came breathless with the task, and the critic pounces on the advance copy. Inside Vereker's work hides a secret figure, and the hunt for it drives the tale.

Glasses, The Next Time, and The Way It Came follow, studies of sight, failure, and return. James writes of writers and their readers with a surgeon's calm. The title is exact: everyone here is caught in some fine, painful awkwardness. These are among his most perfect shorter works, built from talk, glances, and the things people cannot say.
21936-theft-a-play-in-four-acts:
Washington power and a stolen document drive Jack London's play Theft, written in 1910 and set across twenty hours in the capital. Senator Chalmers's wife Margaret stands at the center: twenty-seven, intellectual, womanly, and capable of sudden hardness. Against her father's house stands Howard Knox, a congressman from Oregon with a vision he has followed through abuse and ridicule. The magnate Anthony Starkweather, Margaret's father, holds the purse of the piece.

London, the novelist of the Klondike and the sea, turns to the stage with a socialist's brief. Labor agitators, embassy secretaries, and ministers crowd his cast list. The theft of the title is both a crime and an accusation about wealth itself. It is a fiery, talky period play, more argued than acted in its afterlife.
22112-a-child-s-book-of-saints:
William Canton retold the lives of the saints for young readers in A Child's Book of Saints. Canton, a poet and historian of the Bible Society, had a gift for simple, musical English. His saints are presented as friends and heroes for children to love. Martyrs, hermits, kings, and maidens appear in short, clear chapters.

Each life stresses a single virtue: courage, patience, charity, or faith under scorn. Canton avoids both gore and dryness, keeping wonder in the tales. The book came from an age when saints' stories were standard nursery reading across Britain. It remains a graceful sample of Victorian and Edwardian religious writing for the young.
22293-three-margarets:
Laura E. Richards, daughter of Julia Ward Howe, published Three Margarets in 1897 for girl readers. A pleasant summer rain opens the book, plashing on elms and locusts and tinkling in roadside puddles. On the roof of a great landau rolling toward Fernley House the rain drums less musically. Inside, three girls ride buried in their own thoughts, and each of them is Margaret.

Cousins with one name and three temperaments must live together for a season. Richards builds the story from their contrasts, quarrels, and reconciliations. Her girls' books were famous for sense and humour without preaching. Three Margarets is a gentle specimen, written in her mother's long shadow and her own clear voice.
22314-mysticism-and-its-results:
Mysticism and Its Results is a short book that gathers facts outside the usual range of reading. Its writer asks for the reader's patience at the start. The essay, he says, is suggestive rather than didactic.

That modesty sets the book's method and aim. It does not claim to settle its subject once for all. Instead, it hopes to induce thought, study, or research in honest minds. If it does only that, the writer says, its object will be attained. Readers get an invitation rather than a lecture: a small, earnest case that mystical experience deserves serious, open attention.
22485-devon-its-moorlands-streams-and-co:
Lady Rosalind Northcote wrote Devon: Its Moorlands, Streams, and Coasts. Her book guides readers through England's great western county. Even its opening quotes Shakespeare on Exeter's old castle, Rougemont.

When last at Exeter, the quoted lines run, the mayor showed the castle. He called it Rougemont, at which name the speaker started. An Irish bard had warned he would not live long after seeing Richmond. Such lore flavors Northcote's tour of her home county. Moorland, stream, and coast each get their chapters of attention. Readers get Edwardian local writing at its proudest. Devon appears as history, scenery, and home ground together.
22685-the-classification-of-patents:
The Classification of Patents is a treatise on how patent offices sort inventions into classes so that examiners and inventors can find what came before. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Behind the dry title stands a real problem: hundreds of thousands of patents, useless unless a searcher can find the right shelf.

The author begins at the root: classification lies at the foundation of all mental process. Without seeing resemblances and differences, and grouping things by them, judgment itself is impossible, and reason cannot move from the known to the unknown. From that philosophy the book descends to bins, subclasses, and search practice. It will interest students of information science, who may recognize an early theory of their own field wearing legal dress.
22784-on-laboratory-arts:
Richard Threlfall wrote On Laboratory Arts, a handbook of the mechanical skills behind experimental physics. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Threlfall, an Australian physicist, held that great experiments rest on humble crafts: glassblowing, metalwork, vacuum pumps, and the making of things that cannot be bought.

Experimental work in physical science, he begins, rests in the end upon the mechanical arts. In a well-appointed laboratory the appeal to those arts is often indirect, and a student handed ready apparatus may irresistibly ignore the mechanical basis of the work. The book exists to cure that ignorance. Generations of researchers kept it by the bench, and it remains the classic statement that discovery is also a handicraft.
23173-how-the-raven-died-1902-from-wolfv:
Alfred Henry Lewis dresses two soldiers in How the Raven Died, dated 1902, from Wolfville Nights. This violent person in buckskins, the Old Cattleman says, is a second lieutenant, a mere boy, from West Point. While that outcast in the ridiculous hat is foaled on the plains and never does go that close to the rising sun as to glimpse the Old Missouri. Yet the pair, he swears, are as much alike as the far East is to itself.

Wolfville's narrator spins the tale in the Arizona camp's full dialect, buckskins, West Point, and an Indian called the Raven in one long breath. Lewis's Wolfville books made the mining-camp storyteller a national figure. The Raven's death gets told the camp way, sideways, through likenesses and lies, until the truth stands up in the firelight.
a-brief-bible-history-a-survey-of-the-ol:
A Brief Bible History, published in 1922 by James Oscar Boyd and J Gresham Machen, surveys the history of the Old and New Testaments. The book presents that history as the story of God's redeeming grace. Its chapters trace the stream of God's redeeming purposes flowing down through the older, Old Testament times.

The survey then follows the same purpose broadening and deepening in the New Testament, in Jesus Christ and his Church. Boyd and Machen wrote as Bible teachers, and the book reads as a clear, ordered introduction for students. It gives readers the whole arc of scripture in brief compass, from the first histories to the early church, in one connected account.
a-family-man-in-three-acts:
A Family Man is a play in three acts by John Galsworthy, published in 1922. Galsworthy was an English novelist and playwright, viewed as one of the first writers of the Edwardian era, who challenged the ideals of the society that Victorian literature before him had depicted. He later won the Nobel Prize for Literature, and his Forsyte Saga became his most famous work.

On stage, this play puts a family man at the center of domestic tension. Galsworthy's drama typically sets private comfort against public duty and respectability, and A Family Man works that ground in three acts. The printed play preserves a piece of his Edwardian theatre, from the years when his stage work stood beside his novels in reputation.
a-girl-among-the-anarchists:
Isabel Meredith wrote A Girl Among the Anarchists from inside the London anarchist world she describes, and a preface by Morley Roberts insists that nothing in it is invented. The narrator tells her own story in the first person, beginning with a strange childhood and her arrival among the exiles, printers, and speakers of the movement.

Chapters follow a police scare, a rescue, the office of the paper called the Tocsin, and the escape of a dynamitard. Portraits of anarchist personalities sit beside meetings, flights, and quarrels over what the cause demands. The closing chapters bring a crisis and the last toll of the Tocsin, leaving a rare insider picture of a feared and mostly peaceful circle.
a-list-of-factorial-math-constants: A bare reference table of factorials, computed once by a simple Scheme program whose source code has been lost, as the file's own note explains. It gives every factorial from 1! through 99!, then jumps by hundreds to 900! and by thousands to 10,000!, printing each full value with its digit count. There is no prose beyond the heading notes. The file serves as ready-made big-number data for checking arithmetic, testing software, or satisfying curiosity about how fast factorials grow.
airship-wave-1896-1897-press-accounts:
Seventeen newspaper pieces from 1896 and 1897 make up The Great Airship Wave of 1896-1897, drawn from the Library of Congress's Chronicling America scans. Reports from Sacramento, Oakland, San Francisco, and San Jose open the scare in November 1896. By April 1897 the wave rolled over Kansas, Omaha, and Chicago, with inventors claiming the sky craft as their own.

Editors argued, witnesses swore, and hoaxers confessed in the columns reprinted here word for word. Nothing real was ever found, which makes the papers themselves the true record. The set preserves the primary evidence of America's first great mystery-airship panic, decades before flying saucers.
albertus-magnus-admirables-secrets:
Secrets ascribed to Albert the Great fill this French chapbook of natural magic, in a 1729 printing. Recipes, charms, and wonders of nature promise help with health, love, luck, and beasts. For two centuries it ranked among France's most popular books of hidden knowledge among common folk.

Herbs, stones, and household tricks mix with spells and signs in its pages. Scholars doubt the great Albert wrote a word of it himself. That hardly mattered to the buyers who treasured its lore. The book opens a window on popular belief, where folk magic and medieval science blend without a seam.
anthology-of-massachusetts-poets:
William Stanley Braithwaite gathers the poets of Massachusetts into one anthology, arranged by author. The contents open with Joseph Auslander's Home Bound and Katherine Lee Bates's America the Beautiful and Yellow Clover. Gamaliel Bradford, Alice Brown, Grace Hazard Conkling, and the child poet Hilda Conkling all appear in the early pages.

The poems run from formal odes and sonnets to short lyrics on war, faith, gardens, and Boston streets. Braithwaite, himself a poet and the era's best-known anthologist of new verse, aimed to represent his state's living poetry rather than its classics alone. The book works as a snapshot of New England verse at the moment he made it.
arizona-nights:
Stewart Edward White gathers Western tales told in the voice of men who worked cattle country in Arizona. The table of contents names stories about rustlers, drives, branding, Texas Rangers, buried treasure, and a two-gun man. A storm over the mesas opens the first tale, and the dry land shapes every scene that follows.

The tales move between camp talk and longer linked stories, ending with a long section called The Rawhide. White writes plain speech, hard riding, and desert weather with the ease of a man who knew ranch life. The book preserves the talk and habits of the old Southwest cattle frontier.
balfour-taoist-texts:
Frederic Henry Balfour gathered his Taoist Texts in English in 1884. His anthology sorts the writings by morals, rule, and deep thought. Victorian readers met the philosophy of the Way through books like this.

Short pieces from the Taoist tradition speak in Balfour's clear English. They teach softness over force, quiet rule, and scorn for mere show. Laozi's heirs prize the still mind above wealth and loud fame. Balfour's picks favor calm wisdom over magic and cult practice here. The book stands as an early Western window into Taoist thought and ethics. Its quiet counsel still speaks past its Victorian frame to readers.
beasts-and-super-beasts:
Saki, the pen name of H. H. Munro, gathered Beasts and Super-Beasts in 1914, a book of short stories famous for their polish and bite. Saki sets polite Edwardian drawing rooms against sudden wildness: a hyena loose at a garden party, a cat that may carry a boy's soul, a pig that settles a garden feud. His beasts are often animals, and his super-beasts are often well-dressed people.

The set opens with The Story-Teller, in which a bachelor wins a train carriage of children with a tale about a horribly good little girl who gets eaten by a wolf. The Open Window, with its invented tale of a hunting tragedy, is also here. Few writers pack so much mischief into so few pages.
belinda-an-april-folly-in-three-acts:
A. A. Milne's Belinda, subtitled An April Folly in Three Acts, is a light comedy produced at the New Theatre, London, in April 1918. Belinda Tremayne, her daughter Delia, Harold Baxter, Claude Devenish, John Tremayne and the servant Betty make up its small cast.

The play is set in Belinda's Devonshire country house in late April. The first act plays in the garden, where Betty fastens a hammock for the season, and the later acts move into the hall. Milne, later famous for Winnie-the-Pooh, writes here in the witty, polished manner of the West End stage. Readers who enjoy drawing-room comedy will find Belinda charming and deft.
brandes-eminent-authors-of-the-nineteent:
Brandes set aside his grand survey to write vivid portraits of leading nineteenth-century authors, gathered here in English. Many of his subjects were people he had met or known well. Memory and judgment mix in each sketch.

A portrait by Brandes is no dry summary of dates and books. He seeks the ruling passion of a mind and shows it at work. Praise and blame both come sharp and clear from his pen. The book pairs well with Main Currents, giving readers the critic as portrait painter, working from life as much as from the page.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acceptants:
Acceptants were those Jansenists who accepted the 1713 Bull Unigenitus against Jansenist doctrines in Pasquier Quesnel's Reflexions morales sur le Nouveau Testament, without reserve or mental restriction. Jansenius's error had already caused two conflicts in the church. The first, over his book Augustinus, ended with the Pax Clementina of 1669, also called the false peace. The second, beginning with the eighteenth century, was fought around Quesnel's work.

That work first appeared in 1671, a small volume approved by Vialart, Bishop of Chalons, and grew through editions to four compact volumes by 1693. De Noailles sanctioned it in 1695, then condemned it as Archbishop of Paris the next year. The 1699 edition appeared without the changes Bossuet demanded. Meanwhile the doctrine had taken deep root in the French parliaments and in several religious orders, above all the Oratorians, and the entry follows that spread.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adventists:
Adventists are a group of six American Protestant sects holding in common a belief in Christ's near return in person. They differ mainly in their understanding of doctrines tied to that belief. Except for Seventh Day Adventists and the branch called the Church of God, they are congregational in government. The sects grew from a religious agitation begun by William Miller in 1831, after minute study of Bible prophecies.

Testing Messianic pronouncements by a strictly historical method, Miller looked for every prophecy's fulfilment in its obvious surface reading. Prophecies unfulfilled at Christ's first coming must be fulfilled at his second, when he would return in clouds to possess Canaan and reign a thousand years on David's throne. Counting Daniel's 2,300 days as years from 457 BC, Miller concluded the world would end and Christ return in 1843. When 1843 passed like any other year, his disciple Snow recalculated, and the movement carried on.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-carpets:
Altar carpets ordinarily cover the sanctuary and altar steps of the high altar. Where the floor is marble, tile, or tessellated wood, at least a broad strip lies before the lowest step. Fine rugs are reserved for predella and steps on solemn feasts, and at minimum the high altar's predella, and other altars', should have a rug.

Carpets come off from the Maundy Thursday stripping until Holy Saturday's Mass. During solemn Requiem Masses the sanctuary floor stays bare, though a rug may lie on the predella and before a celebrating bishop's faldstool. Green is mentioned, but any colour may be used. Crosses, saints' images, emblems, and holy monograms must not be woven in, since treading sacred figures underfoot is unbecoming, a rule applying to marble, tile, and mosaic floors too.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anabaptists:
A violent and radical body of church and civil reformers, the Anabaptists first appeared at Zwickau in Saxony in 1521. They still exist in milder forms. Their name joins Greek words for again and baptize, yet they denied that the question was rebaptism at all. They held the first baptism, given in infancy, invalid, and so baptized adults who joined them.

They aimed to restore what they took for primitive Christianity. They rejected oaths, capital punishment, and the magistrate's office, and they held Scripture alone as the rule of faith, though private inspiration counted heavily too. Leaders such as Storch and Munzer in Germany, and Denk and Hubmaier in Switzerland, spread the movement through Augsburg, Nuremberg, and Strasburg. Defeat in the Peasants' War of 1525 scattered its first generation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustinians-:
The Augustinians of the Assumption, also called Assumptionists, are a congregation born at the College of the Assumption in Nimes. Emmanuel d'Alzon, vicar general of the diocese, founded it in 1843. The group was organized in 1847, took first vows in 1850, and won approval by a brief of November 1864. Its aims were to fight irreligion in Europe and schism abroad. To that end it ran schools, used the press, led pilgrimages, and worked missions in the East.

Its Bonne Presse issued periodicals, pamphlets, and books in numbers, chief among them La Croix, printed in several cities. Its apostolic schools trained students for the priesthood free, and in twenty-five years fifteen such houses gave over five hundred priests to the clergy. French resentment led to suppression in 1900, on a charge of hoarding funds for a royalist rising. Many members left France, while their founder, sent to Constantinople in 1863, always declined the episcopate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bachelor-of-a:
The Bachelor of Arts marks the completion of the traditional college curriculum. In medieval universities the Mastership, or Doctorate, stood as the great academic prize. The Bachelorship seems to have grown from using advanced students to teach younger ones. That teaching counted as preparation for the Mastership itself. Before teaching, the student had to defend a thesis in public disputation. That exercise was called Determination, a rehearsal for Inception to the Mastership.

Two examinations tested fitness first: Responsions, then the sterner Examen Baccalariandorum. The Determination rite also gave the student a special cap and a seat among determiners. Pope Gregory IX's bull Parens Scientiarum of 1231 already calls such student-teachers Bachellarii. The word likely came from the guilds, where French Bachelier meant a young apprentice. The long article follows the degree through Oxford, Cambridge, and later systems, with a full source list.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baptists:
Baptists are a Protestant denomination found chiefly in English-speaking countries, named for their doctrine and practice of baptism. They hold Scripture the sufficient and exclusive rule of faith and practice, with each believer free to interpret it. No non-Scriptural scheme binds them, and creeds count only as declarations of prevalent views. Their two chief confessions are the Philadelphia Confession of 1688 and the New Hampshire Confession.

The Philadelphia text revises Westminster (1646) in a Baptist sense, appearing in 1677 and adopted at Philadelphia in 1742. It rules in England and the American South, while the North favors New Hampshire's milder Calvinism, adopted in 1833. Church membership, for Baptists, belongs only to those baptized on a personal profession of faith. They reject infant baptism as contrary to Scripture and accept immersion as the sole valid mode.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-book-of-adver:
The Book of Advertisements, drawn up by Archbishop Matthew Parker with Grindal, Horne, Cox, and Bullingham, set rules for the queen's church ritual. Parker served from 1559 to 1575, helped by four fellow bishops. It matters for the birth of English Nonconformity and for later disputes over ritual law in the 1800s. On Elizabeth's accession in 1558, Latin services and old Catholic rites still stood, while returned exiles pressed for a worship purged of popery.

The 1559 Act of Uniformity imposed the English Prayer-Book, yet its rubric kept Catholic ornaments from Edward VI's second year. Elizabeth's Injunctions overrode the rubric, and the 1559 visit destroyed vestments wholesale. A bishops' meeting in 1560 kept the cope but dropped the crucifix. When Elizabeth demanded one use in 1565, Parker's Book of Articles, twice delayed, appeared in 1566 as the Advertisements, fixing caps, gowns, and surplices against Puritan protest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-act:
In old Roman law, acts were the registers holding official documents and judges' decisions and sentences. In law, acts mean whatever proves or justifies a thing: records, decrees, reports, and certificates. Canonical acts take their name from church procedure. Acts divide into public and private, civil and ecclesiastical. A public act bears certification by a public notary or office-holder, and may be judicial, part of court procedure, or voluntary.

In contested trials the acts should be judicial, while extra-judicial acts are voluntary, not contentious. Both civil and canon law count as public those acts made before witnesses who acknowledge them before the court. An original sealed document from a community, bishop, or public officer, or a duly authenticated copy, counts as a public act. It binds against anyone, though at times it lays no personal duty on non-participants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-imp:
Impedimentum in Latin means whatever embarrasses or hinders a person, and an army's baggage bore the name impedimenta. In law it means whatever bars an agent's free action or keeps him from performing, or performing rightly, an act the law recognizes. It strikes first at the agent's legal capacity, restraining or even suppressing it, and through that at the act itself, which it leaves defective or even null.

An impediment ends when the agent regains capacity, whether by dispensation or by meeting the act's conditions. It may spring from natural law, divine law, or human law, church or civil. Canon law uses impediment in its strict technical sense only for marriage. Bars to holy orders are called irregularities, though some real bars to orders, like being a woman or unbaptized, are not termed irregular at all.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charitable-be:
Charitable bequests turn on what courts count as charity. In the Girard will case, Horace Binney called a charitable gift whatever is given for love of God or love of neighbour, free of personal or selfish motive. A fuller legal definition covers gifts applied under existing law for an indefinite number of people. Such gifts may shape minds through education or religion, relieve disease and suffering, or build public works.

Bequeathing itself has its own history. Blackstone's common law gave one third to heirs, one third to the wife, and one third to the testator's disposal, before statutes widened that power. The Statute of Wills and the end of military tenures under Charles II then freed disposition of real property. Restrictions remain: only persons of sound mind may bequeath, with special rules for infants and married women. A bequest that creates a forbidden perpetuity or makes an estate inalienable fails.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-communion-of-:
Joseph Sollier's entry treats the Communion of Saints, from communio sanctorum, fellowship with the saints. It is the ninth article's second clause in the Apostles' Creed: the Holy Catholic Church, the Communion of Saints. Probably the latest addition to the old Roman Symbol, it appears in the Gallican liturgy, in letters now credited to Caesarius of Arles, in Faustus of Riez, and in Nicetas near 400. Critics built rival theories on these traces, some seeing protest against Vigilantius.

Catholic doctrine reads it as solidarity binding the faithful on earth, souls in purgatory, and saints in heaven in one unity. Early inscriptions show its main forms already alive. Later Fathers gave the full dogma. Sollier follows it through the Anglo-Saxon Church, with its devotion to Mary and heavenly protectors. He follows Protestant views too, closing that revival of the old dogma needs the true doctrine of justification restored beside it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conceptionist:
Michael Bihl's entry follows the Conceptionists, a Clare branch founded by Beatriz de Silva. Isabel of Portugal married John II of Castile and brought kinswoman Beatriz to court. Beautiful Beatriz stirred the queen's jealousy and was imprisoned. Escaping, she fled to Toledo's Dominican sisters, living about forty years there. Devotion to Mary's Immaculate Conception moved her to found an order with twelve companions.

Queen Isabella gave her the castle of Galliana in 1484. The sisters kept the Cistercian rule, adding the Virgin's Office. Beatriz died on 1 September 1490, aged sixty-six. Through Ximenes de Cisneros of Toledo, the order passed under the Franciscans, taking Clare's rule in 1501. Julius II confirmed them in 1506, and Quiñonez framed their constitution in 1516. Houses rose at Torrigo, Madrid, Assisi, Paris. Maria de Agreda, author of The Mystical City of God, wore their white habit, blue cloak, and Marian image.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-confraterniti:
Florence McGahan's entry covers confraternities of penitents, congregations bound by statutes to fasting, discipline, hair shirts, and like works. They multiplied so far, Rome alone counting over a hundred, that only processional garb color sorts them. The garb runs to a heavy robe with girdle and a pointed hood hiding the face, eye holes letting the wearer see unseen. These groups hold their own statues, churches, and often cemeteries. Aspirants serve probation before admission.

White penitents lead with the Archconfraternity of the Gonfalone, founded at Rome in 1264, when Bonaventure served as Inquisitor-general. Black penitents center on the Misericordia, or Beheading of Saint John. Blue, grey, red, violet, and green groups follow, each with its saints and churches. Mixed-color habits defy grouping. Well represented in France from the thirteenth century, these confraternities perhaps flourished most in the sixteenth, when public penance still shaped devotional life.

Henry Parkinson's entry treats local confraternities of priests, apart from the three great ones given entries elsewhere: the Apostolic Union, the Priests' Eucharistic League, and the Priests' Communion League. A confraternity joins persons for a pious object, linked in brotherhood for religion or charity through prayer, example, and counsel. Purely scientific or literary clergy societies fall outside. English diocesan clergy funds, despite duties to living and dead, fall outside too.

A strict priests' confraternity seeks first its members' personal sanctification. Parkinson then tours the lands. Spain, under hostile government, spurred activity, with the Venerable Congregation of Saint Philip Neri. Portugal holds a Lisbon brotherhood from 1415. Austria holds several groups. France holds secular priests of the Sacred Heart at Issoudun. Rome holds the Pia Unio. America holds many agencies for teeming populations. Spanish America holds its own groups. Germany counts some 1,500 members, with Polish priests in their own Unitas insurance society.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-desservants:
An entry on the desservants, a class of French parish priests whose meaning changed with the regime. Under the old order the name meant a priest doing parish duty in a vacant parish or for a censured pastor, the stand-in the Council of Trent wanted in every empty parish. After the Concordat of 1801 it named a second class instead, chosen by the bishop without government sanction and removable by him at any time.

Custom, then law, built the system: Organic Articles set up succursal parishes whose holders were not canonically parish priests and drew no state pay. Bishops and prefects fixed their numbers parish by parish, and efforts to win them full parish rights always failed. French discipline on the point stood fixed, and the Separation Law of 1905 left it standing, though some bishops dropped the old terms.

essays-on-russian-novelists:
Essays on Russian Novelists, by William Lyon Phelps, argues that Russia's greatness rests on its ideas and literature, not its fleets. Phelps opens with the Japanese war, which left Russia's navy destroyed, her armies beaten, her treasury empty, and her pride in the dust. Against that humiliation he sets a question for proud Americans: what have the two nations given the world's literature?

His first essay reads Russian national character through Russian fiction. Russia is old, he notes, yet her literature, so far as the world cares, begins in the nineteenth century, a twin of America's. The essays then take up the great novelists one by one. Phelps writes like a Yale professor lecturing general readers. He asks what each writer saw in the Russian soul. Peasants, officials, and seekers fill their pages, and he explains why. Criticism here is an act of introduction between two young literatures.
father-and-son-a-study-of-two-temperamen:
Edmund Gosse called Father and Son a study of two temperaments and swore in his 1907 preface that every part was scrupulously true. Gosse, son of the naturalist Philip Henry Gosse, grew up inside a strict Puritan household of Plymouth Brethren, where novels, holidays, and doubt itself were sins. The book records the boy's slow, secret emancipation as science and poetry opened doors his father's faith kept locked.

Names are changed, as the preface admits, and comedy mixes with the tragedy of a loving father and son ceasing to speak the same language. Gosse published the memoir anonymously; it became the classic account of Victorian religious childhood. Its calm, funny, devastating tone lets the facts accuse without a raised voice.
ferragus-chief-of-the-de-vorants:
Honore de Balzac's Ferragus, in Katharine Prescott Wormeley's translation, opens a trilogy. With The Duchesse de Langeais and The Girl with the Golden Eyes, it forms The Thirteen. Balzac dedicates the tale to Hector Berlioz. His preface describes thirteen men banded in Paris under the Empire, sworn to one thought and never betraying each other.

Auguste de Maulincour follows a mysterious woman through midnight Paris and is marked for death by the brotherhood. Jules and Clemence Desmarets enjoy one completely happy day, foreboding it their last. Ferragus, a convict become secret sovereign, protects his daughter Clemence from the world. Balzac's Paris of passwords and hidden chiefs starts here.

ghosts-a-domestic-tragedy-in-three-acts:
Henrik Ibsen set Ghosts in a rain-dark house on a Norwegian fjord, in R. Farquharson Sharp's translation. Widow Helen Alving is opening an orphanage built to launder the memory of her husband, a respected captain who lived in secret vice. Her son Oswald, an artist home from Paris, carries his father's disease in his body, and Pastor Manders brings the parish's respectability with him.

Across three acts the dead past takes the house: the captain's sins, a maid's daughter, a fire, and Oswald's final collapse toward the sun he begs to see. Ibsen meant ghosts as inherited ideas as much as inherited illness. The play scandalized Europe in the 1880s and still lands like an accusation against respectable silence.

govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig:
During the Cold War, American agents scoured the globe for enemy hardware they could study. James E. David edited this briefing book, number 616, published in January 2018. Newly declassified documents fill in blanks on that secret search for foreign objects.

The haul ranged from captured MiG fighters to pieces of space junk. Each captured machine taught engineers how Soviet technology really worked, beyond what spies reported. The posting calls scavenging an underreported side of intelligence work. It is a useful corrective: some of the most valuable secrets of the Cold War were not stolen papers but physical objects, hauled home and taken apart.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_mexico_F:
Mexico's Dirty War, decades of state violence against dissidents, went officially unexamined for fifty years. Kate Doyle and Claire Dorfman edited this briefing book, number 879, published in December 2024. It covers the country's first national truth commission and its monumental reports on that violence.

Government archives played an essential role in investigating past abuses, the posting notes. Declassified documents also reveal an American choice: Washington prioritized the stability of the Mexican regime over human rights concerns. The set pairs Mexico's late reckoning with the foreign support that helped delay it, a combination truth commissions rarely document so directly.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
Launch on warning means firing nuclear missiles on the first warning of an enemy attack, before the incoming warheads land. William Burr edited this briefing book, number 674, published in June 2019, updating a 2001 posting. The policy was adopted in the 1970s and remains in effect.

Its danger is the false alert: a sensor error could trigger launch in minutes. A top defense official in 1978 called the policy dangerous, wrong, and ineffective. A Reagan directive, by contrast, aimed to leave Soviet planners with strong uncertainty about the American response. The set preserves an argument among insiders that has never been settled in public.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cyber-vault_Prepa: United States Cyber Command began as a subordinate headquarters and grew into a full combatant command with its own operational force. A National Security Archive briefing book page presents documents tracing that path. They appear under the heading of preparing for computer network operations. They show how USCYBERCOM built, staffed, and trained the teams meant to fight in cyberspace. Only the page capture is preserved in this entry's evidence. The subject itself is foundational, since nearly every later American cyber operation descends from the force-building years these documents describe.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cyber-vault_Silk_:
Silk Road was an online black market where drugs were sold for Bitcoin behind layers of secrecy. Federal agents shut it down in 2013 and 2014, and its founder, Ross Ulbricht, was arrested and prosecuted. A National Security Archive posting from December 2019 turns the lens around and examines the investigators themselves.

Two agents, one from the Drug Enforcement Administration and one from the Secret Service, became targets of corruption investigations tied to their work on the case. That twist made Silk Road a double story: a landmark cybercrime takedown and a warning about the temptations built into undercover work with digital money. Readers get the outline of the massive multi-agency hunt and the scandal that grew inside it, drawn from the released record.
hendershot-1928-press-accounts:
Lester Hendershot, an inventor from Pennsylvania, briefly stunned the press in 1928 with a motor that seemed to run on nothing. Six newspaper reports from that year are gathered here. Five come from the New York Times and one from the New York American, all from February and March.

The reports run from a test flight crowd that included Charles Lindbergh to the slow collapse of the claim. Backers from the Guggenheim fund soon backed away, and experts called the motor a trick. Read in order, the clippings show a free-energy sensation rising and dying in five weeks.
hobson-s-choice-a-lancashire-comedy-in-f:
Hobson's Choice, a Lancashire comedy in four acts by Harold Brighouse, was first produced in America. Its first English production came on June 22, 1916, at the Apollo Theatre, London. The printed cast lists Edyth Goodall as Maggie Hobson. Norman McKinnel played her father, Henry Horatio Hobson, and produced the play. The scene is Salford, Lancashire, and the period is 1880.

Three acts sit in Hobson's boot shop in Chapel Street. The fourth moves to Will Mossop's shop. Hobson is a widowed master shoemaker with three daughters and a love of the pub. Maggie, the eldest, refuses the future he plans. She chooses Will Mossop, his timid best workman, for a husband and a business partner. Brighouse builds the comedy on that choice. The title's phrase means no choice at all. Maggie turns it into the freest decision in the play.
imaginary-portraits:
Walter Pater invented a form in Imaginary Portraits: four studies of artists and thinkers who never quite existed as he shows them. A Prince of Court Painters reconstructs the young Watteau from a friend's journal at Valenciennes in 1701, all sketches, feast days, and early genius. Denys l'Auxerrois brings a medieval god of wine into a French cathedral town, with bloody results.

Sebastian van Storck follows a Dutch follower of Spinoza into cold, abstract devotion, and Duke Carl of Rosenmold ends the book in eighteenth-century Germany. Pater writes slow, jeweled prose, caring more for a temperament's inner weather than for plot. The portraits are really essays on kinds of beauty and belief, and they shaped a generation of aesthetic writers.
in-kedar-s-tents:
In Kedar's Tents, by Henry Seton Merriman, carries an English hero into Spain in a 1909 London edition from Smith, Elder and Co. Merriman's contents move like a campaign map: One Soweth, Another Reapeth, then Like Ships Upon the Sea and Le Premier Pas, the first step. A chapter called Contraband admits the smuggling that runs under the story's politics.

At Ronda and in a Moorish garden the Spanish setting deepens, through a love letter and a war of wit to a city of discontent. Merriman wrote political adventure across Europe and its empires. Here he sets love and conspiracy in a Spain of garrisons, gardens, and mountain roads. The title borrows the psalmist's cry of dwelling far from home among strangers. The novel keeps that exile feeling under its intrigue. Its Englishman stands in uniform, in love, and in danger of choosing wrong.
island-nights-entertainments:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote these three tales of the South Seas in his last years, and the set came out in 1893. He lived then in Samoa, and the isles fill his pages with heat, trade, and old rites. The set's name plays on the tale nights of the Arabian Nights.

'The Bottle Imp' is the gem of the set: a man buys a bottle with an imp that grants all wishes. The catch is grim: who dies with the bottle in hand is damned for good. The rest hold the same mix of charm, dread, and the lore of the isles.
jacobs-incidents:
Harriet Jacobs published Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl in 1861, writing under the name Linda Brent. Jacobs had escaped North years before, but she hid her identity to protect others. Hers is the classic account of slavery as a Black woman lived it.

Jacobs tells how her master harassed her from girlhood and how she resisted. To escape him she hid for seven years in a tiny crawlspace above her grandmother's porch. From there she watched her own children grow below. The book exposed slavery's assault on mothers and families to a wide Northern audience.
kelly-miller-s-history-of-the-world-war-:
Kelly Miller's History of the World War for Human Rights is a 1919 history of the Great War, copyrighted by A. Jenkins. Miller was dean of the College of Arts and Sciences at Howard University. His subtitle explains why America entered the war, states the Allies' cause, and records the part the Negro took in army and navy. Official photographs show devices of modern warfare.

Miller had written Race Adjustment, Out of the House of Bondage, and many pamphlets on social questions. Contributions came from General Pershing, Frederick Drinker, E. A. Allen, and others. The history argues that Black soldiers' service proved their claim to full American rights. It is both a war chronicle and a civil rights brief, written while the ink was fresh.
lectures-on-popular-and-scientific-subje:
The Earl of Caithness delivered these lectures on popular and scientific subjects in many places. Trübner published the second, enlarged edition in London in 1879. The Earl was a fellow of the Royal Society.

Talks treat coal and coal mines, plus science applied to art. One lecture defends thrift: take care of the pence. Others cover the steam engine and past means of travel and news. Caithness writes for general audiences, not specialists. His volume shows how Victorian lords joined the public science movement. A lecture on communication traces roads, posts, and wires. Caithness treats invention as a story for every listener.
legends-of-the-madonna-as-represented-in:
Anna Jameson wrote Legends of the Madonna as part of her Sacred and Legendary Art series. Houghton Mifflin issued this corrected, enlarged edition at Boston in 1881. Publishers note that Jameson died before revising this edition herself.

She explains how artists pictured Mary across the centuries. Paintings, sculptures, and church images guide her chapters. Stories behind the images matter as much as the art itself. Jameson helped English readers learn to read religious pictures. Her warm, learned style made art history welcoming to newcomers. Her earlier Sacred and Legendary Art volumes stand behind it. Jameson treats painters as storytellers in line and color.
legge-the-chinese-classics-vol-1-confuci:
Confucius speaks in the Analects, the heart of the first volume of Legge's Chinese Classics, printed with the Chinese text. Short sayings and brief talks with disciples fill the book. Virtue, learning, good rule, and the good life form its steady themes.

Legge's Victorian version, fruit of years in China, opened the Master to the English world. Rulers hear that kindness and rite, not force, hold a state together. Students hear that learning begins with honesty about what one knows. The Analects shaped East Asian life for two thousand years, and Legge's labor remains a monument of the field.
lollingdon-downs-and-other-poems-with-so:
John Masefield published this poetry volume with Heinemann in 1917. He dedicates the poems and sonnets to his wife. Companion volumes include Dauber, The Daffodil Fields, and Philip the King. The Faithful, a play, shares the uniform edition list.

The opening poem counts life as beads of coloured days. The self, Masefield writes, is the string holding them. Lollingdon Downs gives the collection its title and landscape. Sonnets accompany the longer poems throughout the volume. The Faithful, his play, shares the uniform volume list. Dauber and The Daffodil Fields precede Philip the King there.
macmillan-co-s-general-catalogue-of-work:
Macmillan and Co.'s General Catalogue, dated December 1869, lists their books for sale. It covers history, biography, travels, and belles lettres. Each entry carries some short account of the critical notices it won. Names here include Gladstone, Guizot, Kingsley, Freeman, and John Morley.

A publisher's catalogue is a map of what one age read. Macmillan stood among London's most respected houses in 1869. Their list mixes sermons, scholarship, novels, and tales of travel. Prices and praise helped booksellers and readers choose new works. Today the catalogue serves historians of Victorian reading. It shows the taste of a book-buying public long vanished.

make-your-own-hats:
Make Your Own Hats is a millinery manual by Gene Allen Martin. Houghton Mifflin published it in 1921, with drawings by E. E. Martin. Martin directed domestic arts at the Minneapolis Y.W.C.A. She also designed and taught hat-making for many students.

The first chapters cover equipment, materials, and velvet-covered frames. Frames of neteen, crinoline, and wire each get full treatment. Later lessons turn to shaping, trimming, and finishing hats at home. The book assumes a home sewer with patience and taste. It preserves the craft behind the grand hats of 1921. Modern makers still learn from such clear, careful manuals.
marjorie-s-three-gifts:
Marjorie's Three Gifts is a short story by Louisa May Alcott. Roberts Brothers' Boston edition here dates from 1899. Marjorie sits on the doorstep shelling peas into a bright tin pan. Roses peep at her through the porch lattice, and robins wish her happy birthday.

She hears none of it, for her thoughts are far away. Last night granny told her a fairy tale of gifts. A poor girl at her spinning received a good-luck penny from a Brownie. Then a fairy passed, with a gift of her own. Alcott lets Marjorie's birthday wish meet the old tale's magic. The Little Women author writes with her usual tender wisdom.
memories-and-portraits:
Robert Louis Stevenson gathered Memories and Portraits in a set of papers. Chatto and Windus printed this fine paper edition in London in 1912. He gave the book to his mother, in past joy and present sorrow.

His note says the papers hang together more than they seem. Memories of youth and portraits of the dead build one face. That face, he found, was his own young self, long lost. He was the first to be surprised by that turn, he admits. A steamer note, written within sight of Cape Race, dates the gift. Read in order, he urges, not dipped into at random.
men-women-and-boats:
Vincent Starrett edited this posthumous collection of Stephen Crane's stories and sketches. He gathered the pieces from out-of-print books and old magazine files. Some tales appear between covers here for the first time. The title was the editor's own choice, as his note explains.

The centerpiece is The Open Boat, Crane's celebrated tale of shipwrecked men at sea. Around it stand war sketches, city pieces, and early experiments like A Dark Brown Dog. The editor regrets that copyright problems forced out The Blue Hotel. For readers, the volume recovers minor Crane works that had nearly vanished from print.
men-women-and-ghosts:
Amy Lowell's book gathers narrative poems rather than lyrics, as her preface explains. She calls them stories, stretched to the widest sense of the word. Some are tales in scenes, while others make characters of air, clouds, and streets. The poems use the free rhythms of vers libre throughout.

Lowell says Debussy's piano music showed her how movement could shape a poem. She experiments with rhythm the way a musician varies tempo and theme. Poems like A Roxbury Garden try to copy the motion of rolling hoops and growing plants. The book shows an American modernist testing what free verse could do.
mercadet-a-comedy-in-three-acts:
Honoré de Balzac wrote this comedy in three acts, first staged in Paris in August 1851. The scene is a Paris house around 1845. Mercadet, a speculator, owes money to a crowd of creditors. His daughter Julie has a suitor, De la Brive, whose fortune matters greatly to the family.

Creditors like Goulard, Pierquin, and Violette press at the door from the first scene. Even the servants joke that their master is sure to drown. Mercadet schemes, stalls, and charms his way through each new demand. Balzac turns debt and speculation into fast, sharp stage comedy.
miscellaneous-mathematical-constants:
Simon Plouffe compiled this reference collection of mathematical constants at Simon Fraser University. Each number is computed to hundreds or thousands of digits. Entries range from one over pi squared, to five thousand digits, to the cosine of one at fifteen thousand digits. The file was downloaded from the Inverse Symbolic Calculator project's tables.

Named constants include Artin's, Catalan's, Champernowne's, and the Copeland-Erdos constant. Roots, exponentials, and zeta values fill out the list. The collection serves programmers and researchers who need exact digits for checking calculations. Plouffe later became known for formulas computing pi's digits, and this file shows his early precision work.
modern-religious-cults-and-movements:
Gaius Glenn Atkins, a Congregational minister and author, wrote this survey of America's new religions. His publisher's description lists the movements drawing crowds for two decades past. They include faith healing, Christian Science, and New Thought. Theosophy and spiritualism complete the set.

Atkins brought, his reviewers said, a firm grasp of Christian belief to the task. He wrote with clarity about movements many churchgoers found confusing or threatening. His other books ranged from Jerusalem's history to studies of the great mystics. This volume asks what needs the cults meet, and how the older churches should answer them.
mr-pim-passes-by-a-comedy-in-three-acts:
A. A. Milne wrote this comedy in three acts for the stage. The cast lists George Marden, his wife Olivia, and niece Dinah. Lady Marden, Brian Strange, and Carraway Pim complete the house party. The scene is the morning room at Marden House in Buckinghamshire.

Milne first staged the play in Manchester and then in London. A passing remark by Mr. Pim shakes the calm house. Old ties and young love are thrown into doubt. The mix-up is handled with light talk and neat turns. It shows Milne the playwright, years before his bear books made him most famous.
mrs-budlong-s-christmas-presents:
Rupert Hughes published this comic novel in 1912, set in the small town of Carthage. The story opens the morning after Christmas Eve. The whole house feels the ache of gifts given, missed, and received. Folks must smile and cry out that each gift is just right.

Hughes notes that Carthage folk are not rich, so gifts run small. Some are useless, and some are far too useful. Chapter titles promise schemes, foiled plans, and an amazing Christmas. Mrs. Budlong stands at the center of the giving and scheming. The book is a warm, sharp comedy about pride, love, and holiday gifts gone wrong.
music-as-a-language-lectures-to-music-st:
Ethel Home, head mistress of Kensington High School, gave these lectures to music students. Oxford's Clarendon Press issued the book in 1916. Her title claims music is a language to be taught with care. The first lecture treats the training of the music teacher.

Later lectures cover school programs, voice work, and the sol-fa method. Ear training, sight singing, rhythm, and dictation each get a chapter. She ends with harmony and first steps in composition. Home writes for teachers, not performers. Her plan shows how music was taught in British schools, step by plain step.
my-war-experiences-in-two-continents:
S. Macnaughtan's war memoir was edited by her niece after her death. John Murray issued it in London in 1919. The niece, Mrs. Lionel Salmon, shaped the letters and notes. A portrait by E. O. Hoppe fronts the volume.

The title promises war work on two continents. Macnaughtan, a novelist, went out to aid troops and the wounded. Her dedication follows a wish she had voiced herself. The book mixes letters, diary notes, and sharp witness. It shows the home front and the war zones through one tireless woman's eyes, kept in print by her family's care.
nasa-tm-19630006831-observational-astrop:
Theodore P. Stecher and James E. Milligan of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this paper. They gave it at the COSPAR meeting in May 1962. It reports star studies made from sounding rockets. Earth's air blocks ultraviolet light, so rockets carried the tools above it.

The paper opens by noting air is opaque below a set wavelength. Rocket flights caught ultraviolet spectra, the rainbow of starlight spread out. Observed light was checked against model stellar atmospheres. Light soaked up between the stars was part of the study. These short rocket hops opened a new window on hot stars before space telescopes flew.
nasa-tm-19650010094-scientific-explorati:
An address given on October 5, 1964, at Worcester Polytechnic Institute forms the core of this record. The speaker returned to Worcester for the institute's centennial convocation luncheon. Hugh L Dryden, NASA's deputy administrator, had been prevented from attending, the address notes.

Its subject is what the scientific exploration of space demands of education. A new field needs trained people, and schools must supply them. The speech speaks to that challenge in general terms for a general audience. It preserves how space leaders made the education case in public in 1964. Heard today, it also records the hopes and worries that space flight raised for schools at that moment.
nasa-tm-19660011717-ego-orbital-paramete:
H E Montgomery and S J Paddack, in Goddard's Theoretical Division, computed orbit data and heat inputs for the EGO satellite in April 1963. EGO was part of the Orbiting Geophysical Observatory family, called OGO in the catalog note. Their work gives orbital parameters over time, the spacecraft's changing angles, and the heat flowing into it from Sun and Earth.

Heat input decides a satellite's temperature balance in orbit. Designers need that input for each point of the path, not just an average. The authors present both their methods and their results. Other teams could then check thermal designs against real numbers, rather than rough guesses, for a large observatory satellite.
nasa-tm-19660028661-c2-swan-bands-in-com:
Ralph E. Stockhausen and Donald E. Osterbrock study comet light in this paper. Comets glow with bright bands of light from carbon molecules, called the C2 Swan bands. The authors ask how the molecules' vibration levels are populated when sunlight excites them, a process called fluorescence.

They calculate those populations two ways and get similar results. One way is a rough three-level shortcut; the other solves the balance equations for ten levels. Their excitation temperatures match published comet observations well. They also estimate the infrared glow from the same process in a bright comet, and find it small and hard to detect.
nasa-tm-19670012131-polarization-and-int:
Donald F. Heath, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in March 1967. It reports rocket measurements of hydrogen Lyman alpha light in the day airglow, the faint ultraviolet glow of the upper atmosphere. Heath measured both the light's intensity and its polarization, a measure theorists had flagged as key to the hydrogen problem.

A far ultraviolet polarization photometer with many channels recorded intensity and polarization against altitude for several emission features. These included the Lyman alpha line, atomic oxygen lines, and an unnamed glow at longer wavelengths. The instrument flew on an Aerobee 150 rocket launched from White Sands, New Mexico, on August 29, 1966. Partner experiments on the same flight measured direct solar Lyman alpha, broadband solar flux, and electron density and temperature.
nasa-tm-19670022480-pressure-and-heat-tr:
John O. Reller Jr. and H. Lee Seegmiller, of NASA's Ames Research Center in California, measured what flight does to a Mercury capsule shape. Their memorandum, TM X-647, reports pressure and heat-transfer measurements on a model of the Mercury capsule, the first American crewed spacecraft. Knowing the heating on its blunt heat shield was vital to a safe return through the atmosphere.

The program spread across three kinds of facilities: wind tunnels, shock tunnels, and free flight. Separate sections describe the models and instrumentation used in each setting. Data reduction chapters treat the calibration of the air streams, chemical equilibrium in the flow around the model. Other chapters treat heat-transfer data reduction and collected flow visualization. Results and discussion then take up the stagnation region, the heat shield, and the rest of the capsule surface in turn.
nasa-tm-19670030839-station-contact-time:
F. O. Vonbun, of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston, Texas, compiled this data paper in November 1964. It gives station contact times for Apollo orbits with variable launch azimuths. A contact time is the window during which a ground station can hear and talk to a spacecraft. Mission planners needed those windows in advance.

The paper presents graphs of contact times for the Apollo spacecraft in its parking orbits around Earth. Two orbit heights are considered, roughly two hundred and three hundred kilometers up. The graphs cover one to six parking orbits and show each ground station's windows as the launch azimuth swings across its full range. When a launch slips, the azimuth changes continuously with the delay. Vonbun hoped the graphs would help solve the tracking and communication tasks that such shifting orbits create.
nasa-tm-19680024113-variable-geometry-re:
Milton A. Beheim and Aaron S. Boksenbom of Lewis Research Center wrote this 1968 paper, TM X-52447, for an aeronautical sciences congress in Munich, Germany. They examine why jet inlets and exhaust nozzles for very fast aircraft must change shape in flight. A shape that works well above the speed of sound performs badly below it, they note.

Fixed shapes bring heavy pressure losses and drag at the speeds they were not built for. Lewis tests therefore compared round inlets first, with flat two-sided designs also prepared. The team varied how compression splits between outside and inside surfaces, and tried plug nozzles as well. They stress that results were still incomplete, so their conclusions stay tentative.
nasa-tm-19690010670-gamma-ray-astronomy-:
C. E. Fichtel, D. A. Kniffen, and H. B. Ogelman of Goddard Space Flight Center report gamma ray astronomy balloon results in this February 1969 paper, X-611-69-58. Balloons lift Goddard's digitized spark chamber telescope above most of the air. From that height it can catch gamma rays, the most energetic form of light, arriving from space.

The team reanalyzed data on the galactic center, hunting a possible line source in the galactic plane. Their value alone does not justify claiming a detection, they state, though it fits a satellite result. They also measured the atmospheric background glow from many angles. Upper limits on point sources fell below simple forecasts, and no positive point source evidence was found.
nasa-tm-19690030728-the-topside-ionosphe:
S. J. Bauer, R. E. Hartle, and J. R. Herman, of Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this October 1969 preprint, X-615-69-459. Their subject is the topside ionosphere of Venus and its interaction with the solar wind. Mariner V's two-frequency radio occultation experiment had watched the daytime ionosphere end abruptly. Venus has no strong magnetic shield, so the wind strikes that layer directly.

The authors picture solar wind magnetic fields piling up atop the conducting ionosphere. That magnetic obstacle, a kind of pseudo-magnetopause, raises a bow shock in the supersonic wind. Evidence came from both Mariner V and Venera IV. Using measured wind properties, they estimate the shocked gas and field buildup. Pressure balance at the cutoff, they show, fits the sharp electron density edge.
nasa-tm-19700022716-optimum-launch-traje:
Omer F. Spurlock and Fred Teren of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 astrodynamics conference in Santa Barbara, California. It finds the best launch trajectories for the ATS-E mission. ATS-E was an Applications Technology Satellite bound for a high orbit.

The authors obtained the optimum paths and present their analysis, steps, and results. Each path is computed from launch to insertion into the final orbit. Because the apogee motor was much smaller than the optimum size, the standard profile had to change. Their adjusted paths yield the greatest payload the smaller motor can deliver.
nasa-tm-19710012124-analytical-studies-o:
Theodore L. Felsentreger and James P. Murphy wrote this NASA preprint in March 1971 on luni-solar effects, the slow pulls of the Moon and Sun on artificial satellites. Those pulls gradually change a satellite's orbital elements, the numbers that describe its path. Predicting them matters for keeping spacecraft on station and for reading tracking data correctly.

The study works out perturbations in the orbital elements and compares them with effects from Earth's own gravity field. It then applies the analysis to real spacecraft: Relay 1, Telstar 2, and Relay 2. Separate sections treat shadow effects on Telstar 2, when Earth blocks the Sun's pull, and seasonal variations in Earth's gravity field. Figures track eccentricity and inclination changes for the Relay and Telstar satellites.
nasa-tm-19720017235-apollo-14-some-geoch:
Apollo 14: Some Geochemical Aspects reports the chemistry of Moon samples brought home by the Apollo 14 mission. The scan does not render its author names legibly. Apollo 14 was the first mission to visit an uplands region, away from the dark mare plains. Its landing site sat in the Fra Mauro Formation, debris thrown out by the impact that formed the Imbrium basin.

Chemical analyses covered five soil samples, three core samples, a soil clod, two breccia rocks, a basalt, and separated mineral phases. The samples proved strikingly uniform in chemistry, pointing to thorough mixing or uniform source rocks. The basalt could be matched by a mixture of about four parts soil to one part plagioclase. The authors found the samples chemically kin to Apollo 12 and 15 KREEP material, and suggested that mare basalts may represent fused cumulates.
